OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN. Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away 
of Swami Ranganathananda, President of the Ramaknshna Math and Mission on the 25th 
April, 2005 following a cardiac arrest. 
Born in the village of Trikkur in Kerala in December, 1908, Swamiji joined the Ramaknshna 
Order at its centre in Mysore in 1926 at the age of 18 years. 
He became the President of the Rama kriahna Math and the Ramakrishna 
Mission in September, 1998. 
Swami Ranganathananda undertook extensive lecture tours covering fifty countries. He 
was India's foremost Cultural Ambassador. Through his writings and lectures, the West 
imbibed the spirit of ancient Indian seers. 
He was one of the foremost modern exponents of the Vedanta. 
In the death of Swami Ranganathananda, the country has lost an icon of sublime 
spirituality. 
I request hon. Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect 
to the memory of the departed soul. 
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute]

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
Strengthening of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
*441. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI 
RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any steps have been or are being taken by the authorities of various 
States to demarcate the functional areas of the different tiers of local bodies in 
order to strengthen the Panchayati Raj Institutions; 
(b) if so, the details of such steps taken as on date, State-wise, category-wise and 
year-wise; 
(c) whether any steps have been or are being taken to transfer the 
Institutions and staff under Government to the Panchayati Raj Institutions; 
(d) if so, the details of such steps taken as on date, State-wise; and 
(e) other steps taken to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions and the present 
status of such Institutions as on date State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANISHANKARAIYAR): 
(a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The details are set out in Statement I (See below). 
(d) With a view to accelerating the pro cess of activity mapping, there has 
been intensive interaction between the Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj and 
several of the State Governments concerned, the outcome is summarized at 
statement-ll (See below). 
(e) The question of the effective devolution of functions, functionaries and 
finances was taken up at the first Round Table of State Panchayati Raj 
Ministers held in Kolkata in July, 2004. The conclusions reached by consensus 
may be seen at Statement-Ill (See be low). To monitor the implementation of 
these consensual conclusions, the Union Minister of Panchayati Raj will be 
visiting all States and Union Territories. A Committee of Secretaries has been 
constituted to meet approximately once a month and a Council of Panchayati Raj 
Ministers will be reviewing implementation periodically.

Statement-Ill 
First round table of Ministers-in-Charge of Panchayati Raj Kolkata 
24-25th July, 2004 
Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj, and their representatives, bearing in mind the spirit 
of cooperative federalism which must inform the effective implementation of Panchayati Raj 
as set out in Para IX of the Constitution of India and related provisions, including in particular, 
Article 243ZD (District Planning Committees), agreed to recommend to their 
respective Governments, for joint acceptance by the Centre and the States, the 
following points of action:— 
Effective Devolution of Functions: 
(i) The Constitution (Article 243G) provides for "devolution", that is, the empowerment 
of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) to function as institutions of self-government for the 
twin purposes of (i) making plans for economic development and social justice for 
their respective areas, and ii) implementing programmes of economic development and 
social justice in their respective areas, for subjects devolved to the PRIs, including those 
listed in the Eleventh Schedule, and subject to such conditions as the State may, by 
 law, specify. Therefore, the key objective is to ensure that 
Panchayati Raj Institutions function as institutions of self-government 
rather than as mere implementing agencies for other authorities in respect of such 
functions as may be devolved on them; 
(ii) while devolution must eventually comprise the entire range of subjects 
provided for in the State legislation in a time-bound manner, States/UTs may 
prioritize their devolution programme to ensure that for such functions as are 
prioritized, there is full and effective devolution in empowering PRIs as 
institutions of self-government in respect of these functions: 
(iii) To this end,the essential step is the identification of activities related to the 
devolved functions with a view to attributing each of these activities to the 
appropriate tier of the 3-tier system. To the extent possible, there should be no 
overlapping between tiers in respect of any given activity; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
(iv) In determining the tier of the Panchayati Raj System to which any given activity is 
to be attributed, the principle of subsidiarity must, to the extent possible, be 
followed. The principle of subsidiarity states that any activity which can be 
undertaken at a lower level must be undertaken at that level in preference to being 
undertaken at any higher level; 
(v) On the basis of the identification of activities relating to devolved functions, and 
through the application of the principle of the subsidiarity, States/UTs may 
review/undertake time-bound activity mapping with a view to completing this 
exercise within the fiscal year 2004-05; 
(vi) The activity mapping model .as evolved in the Ministry of Rural Development 
in the Report of the Task Force on Devolution of Powers and Functions upon 
Panchayati Raj Institutions, and the information provided about existing State-wise 
activity mapping in the Fact Sheets presented to the Round Table, might be 
drawn upon by State Govemments/UT Administrations for preparing their 
respective activity mapping exercises; 
(vii) The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj could, on request, furnish technical 
assistance and expertise to State Govts./UT Administrations to 
accomplish activity mapping within the timeframe indicated; 
(viii) With a view to promoting a measure of irrevocabiKty of devolved functions, 
devolution may be routed through legislative measure or, alternatively, by 
providing a strong legislative framework for devolution thro ugh 
executive orders. 
Effective Devolution of Functionaries: 
(I) The devolution of functionaries to the Panchayati Raj Institutions should be 
patterned on the activity mapping of activities related to devolved functions; 
(II) Where the devolved activity requires the deputation of State Government 
officials to assist the elected PRI in planning or implementing the devolved 
activity, the officials concerned must be primarily responsible to, and under the 
disciplinary supervision and control of, the elected authority; 
(III) With a view to building a cadre of officials and technocrats specialized 
in the devolved functions of the PRIs, State Governments/UT 
Administrations may consider instituting a 
8 

[26 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Panchayati Raj Administrative and Technical Service, with the . State 
Government discontinuing further recruitment of staff to State services for such 
devolved functions; 
(IV) (i) Reconceiving the role of District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) 
as an important instrument for Panchayati Raj development through the 
progressive merger of DRDAs with the District Panchayats. The technical 
expertise and other facilities of the DRDAs should become available to all 
tiers of the PRIs under the overall responsibility and disciplinary control of 
the elected authority in the PRIs at the appropriate level; 
(ii) The activities of the reconceived DRDAs with respect to the three tiers of 
the Panchayati Raj system should be patterned on the activity map for the 
devolution of functions, functionaries and funds so that all the three tiers of 
PRIs have equitable access to the resources, expertise, facilities and 
manpower of the DRDAs. 
Effective Devolution of Finances: 
(I) The "sound finances" of the Panchayats is a Constitutional obligation 
enjoined on the States by Article 243-1. In pursuance of this Constitutional 
obligation, the States and the Centre, in a true spirit of fiscal federalism, should 
work together to strengthen the finances of the elected local bodies; 
(10 To this end, the devolution of finances to the three tiers of the Panchayati Raj 
System should be patterned on activity mapping for the devolution of functions 
and functionaries, thus securing effective devolution of powers to the PRIs 
through the linking of the devolution of finances to the devolution of 
functions and functionaries; 
(III) On the basis of the principles adumbrated above, the State Governments 
might attempt to prepare a road map, to be made effective as soon as 
possible, and, in any case, by the end of the next fiscal year 2005-06, which 
might include the following components: 
(i) Devolution, tier-wise and based on activity mapping, of: 
(a) Planning; 
(b) Budgeting; 
(c) Provisioning of finances. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
(ii) Inclusion of a PRI component in the budget of each State/Central Government 
department based on activity mapping; 
(iii) Provision of progressively larger untied funds, tier-wise, to the Panchayats 
by State/Central Governments; 
(iv) Provision of untied grants from the Planning Commission to the PRIs, tier-
wise, based on activity mapping; 
(v) Tier-wise allocations, based on activity mapping of the PRIs, of hitherto 
unallocated grants, if any, made by previous Finance Commissions, and a 
pre-determined pattern for the tier-wise allocation within a time-bound 
framework of grants from the 12th and future Finance Commissions; 
(vi) A schedule, to be determin ed by each State Government/ UT 
Administration, of the time-frames within which State Finance Commissions 
should prepare their reports; for the submission of State Finance Commission 
recommendations, along with Action Taken Reports (ATRs), to the 
Legislature; and for the executive to act on recommendations/ATRs endorsed by 
the State Legislature; 
(vii) Steps to encourage PRIs to raise their own resources, especially through the 
provision to "appropriate" revenues raised by them for their own purposes 
(Article 243 H). 
Gram Sabhas: 
(i) Article 243A of Part IX of the Constitution provides for the establishment 
of Gram Sabhas to "exercise such powers and perform such functions at the 
village level as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide"; 
(ii) A strong system of Gram Sabhas is the indispensable foundation of good 
governance through Panchayati Raj; 
(iii) Based on the two principles stated above, State Governments may review the 
extant legislation to determine the legislative and other steps which remain to be 
taken to ensure that the "powers" and "functions" mentioned in Article 243A of 
the Constitution are adequately incorporated in the State legislation. In 
particular, the following points may be examined:- 
(i) The need for constituting Sabhas below the Gram level (such as Gram 
Sansad, Upa-Gram Sabha or Ward Sabha, by whatever 
10 

[26 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
name called) with the aim of ensuring that the adult population in each ward is 
given the opportunity of conveying to the Gram Sabha their views on issues 
coming up for consideration as also holding the elected Ward representative 
responsible to the adult population in each Ward; 
(ii) The periodicity of meetings of Gram Sabhas and Ward Sabhas; 
(iii) Provision for full and satisfactory consultation with special or disadvantaged 
categories of the population, such as women, SC/ ST, landless labourer etc; 
(iv) Provision for Mahila Sabha meetings, comprising all the adult women of a 
Ward/Gram Panchayat area, to deliberate upon, and decide the modalities of, 
expressing their views in the Gram/Ward Sabhas; 
(v) Endowing the Gram/Ward Sabha with meaningful empowerment through 
such measures as: 
(a) Right/entitlement to all the information required for the Gram/ Ward 
Sabhas to contribute to transparent and good governance, as well as to make the 
elected Panchayat truly answerable to the Gram/Ward Sabha; 
(b) Approve before implementation commences, plans and programmes 
(including budgets) for economic development and social justice prepared by 
the Gram Panchayat; 
(c) Authorize the issuance of utilization certificates of funds allocated for 
the plans, projects or programmes of the Panchayat; 
(d) Identification of beneficiaries. 
(vi) Such social audit measur es may also be appropriately 
institutionalized at the Block and District level.

†*442. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the World Bank has inspected and assessed the 
ongoing projects to uplift the standard of living of the villagers of backward districts of 
Madhya Pradesh under District Poverty Initiatives Programme (DPIP) and World Bank has 
appreciated the success of the projects; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government are considering to seek more assistance from the World Bank 
for extending the projects in Madhya Pradesh and in other states; and 
(d) if so, the details of the steps taken/proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) 
Government has noted the assessment of the World Bank that Madhya Pradesh District 
Poverty Initiatives Project (MP-DPIP) is moving in the right direction of achieving the 
development objectives. However, this project's utilization of the World Bank assistance needs 
to be accelerated by the State Government as only 40.6% of the credit has been utilised till 
March, 2005. 
(c) and (d) In the Country Strategy for India (CAS) of the World Bank for the period 
2005-08, six Rural Livelihood projects have been identified, covering the states of 
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. One State is yet to be 
identified.

Allocation of funds to check declining ground water level 
†*447. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the State-wise total amount allotted during the last year by Government to 
check the declining ground water level in the country; 
(b) the details of the ratio of declining ground water level during last three years, 
State-wise; and 
(c) the amount allocated to different NGOs, State-wise during the last one year for 
this purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYA RANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (c) Ministry of Water Resources was not having any approved 
scheme during the last year to check the declining ground water level in the country. 
"Water" being a State subject, it is the primarily the responsibility of the concerned 
State Governments to take steps to check the declining ground water level. However, the 
following steps have been taken by the Union Government in this direction:— 
(i) A scheme at an estimated cost of Rs. 175 crores for Artificial Recharge to 
Ground Water and Rain Water Harvesting for implementation during the 
remaining part of the Tenth Five Year Plan is under consideration. 
(ii) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to the 
State/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area specific artificial 
recharge schemes to check the declining trend of ground water levels. 
(iii) Central Ministries/Departments of Railways, Defence, Posts, 
Telecommunications, Central Public Works Department and National 
Highways Authority of India have been requested to provide roof top rain 
water harvesting structures in the buildings under their control. 
(iv) States/UTs have been requested to provide water harvesting structures in 
buildings under their administrative control. 
(v) All the States/Union Territories have been requested for advising the local 
bodies in their respective States/Union Territories to 
†Ortginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
20 

[26 April, 2005] RAJYA  SABHA 
allow rebate in property tax to persons, who adopt roof top rainwater 
harvesting in their premises. 
(vi) CGWB has provided technical guidance on rain water harvesting to around 1800 
agencies, including State Government agencies, educational Institutions, private 
entrepreneurs and individuals. 
(vii) Launching of a website on Roof Top Rain Water Harvesting 
(www.cgwb.net) to make aware and educate the public about various 
techniques of harvesting rainwater and store it for future use. 
(viii) Organisation of mass awareness programmes and training courses on rainwater 
harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(ix) Rain Water Harvesting campaign has been launched keeping in view the various 
target groups like youth and children, women, farmers and villagers, policy 
and opinion makers. Publicity through print media, telecasting of spots 
on the television, broadcasting messages on radio, holding of 
seminars, workshops, conferences etc., have been undertaken for the 
purpose. 
(x) The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation, Government 
of India have amended Building Bye-laws, 1983, making provision for water 
harvesting through storing of water run-off including rain water in all new 
buildings on plots of 100 square meters and above in Delhi mandatory. 
Similarly, State Governments of Tamil Nadu. Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, 
Rajasthan and Kerala have made roof top rain water harvesting mandatory in 
specified cases. 
The ground water level data collected by CGWB through a network of observation 
wells is analyzed and declining trend is determined based on the data of one decade. During 
the last decade (1995-2004), significant decline (more than 20 cm/year) in ground water 
levels during the pre-monsoon period has been observed in parts of 362 districts of 23 
States/ UTs details of which are enclosed as Statement (See below). 
As there was no fund for NGO based scheme in the Ministry of Water Resources during 
the last year for the purpose of checking declining ground water table, no amount was allotted 
to NGOs for this purpose.

†*448. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that imposition of 4 per cent tax on salt has created a 
crisis for over 25 lakhs of farmers and labourers engaged in production of salt; 
†Ortginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
24 

[26 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether Government are considering or propose to remove tax on salt by 
amending the salt policy; 
(c) if so, the details thereof;

farmers and labourers engaged in production of salt; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and by when these steps will be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) VAT is a 
tax intended to replace the State Sales Tax. Hence, the Central Government has no role to 
play either in imposing VAT on any particular item or exempting any item from VAT An 
Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers was set up to decide on all issues 
relating to implementation of State level VAT.

Penalty on airlines on cancellation of flights 
3412. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: W ill the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to impose heavy penalities on any domestic or 
international airlines who cancel their scheduled flights without proper intimation 
except bad climate; 
(b) if so, by when it will be started; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI 
PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (c) There is presently no proposal to impose heavy penalties on any 
domestic or international airlines in the event of cancellation of flights. The present 
international air law as established by Warsaw Convention and Montreal Convention, 
1999 envisage only a measure of facilitation and do not contemplate any punitive action 
against airlines in case of cancellation/postponement of flights. Most airlines in India 
already have procedures in place for providing standard passenger facilitation measures in 
the event of delay/postponement of flights and do everything within their means to ensure 
that stranded passengers are not inconvenienced. Besides, because of the very nature of the air 
transportation industry, safety considerations have to be given foremost priority and 
reasons for delay of the flights are often beyond the control of the airlines. Any punitive 
provision may also end up increasing the cost of air travel considerably as airlines may be 
compelled to pass on a part of the financial burden to the passengers.

eradication? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, sir. 
(b) The focus of the report is on fiscal  reforms needed to increase the 
development effectiveness at the State level. The keys areas deliberated in the 
report are (i) reducing deficits which have grown to unsustainable levels; (ii) 
restructuring expenditure to increase expenditures in productive areas, and reduce

3506. DR. ALLADI P. RAJ KUMAR: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the estimated annual loss to exchequer due to adulteration of petrol, diesel 
and lubricants in the country as per information available with the Ministry; and 
(b) what efforts have been made to reduce the adulteration at various levels i.e., from 
refinery to retail sale and how far these efforts have been successful in checking the 
adulteration? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) While, the Government is aware of attempts by unscrupulous 
elements to adulerate petroleum products, no estimate of annual loss to exchequer due 
to this is available. 
The action taken by the Government/Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) in containing the menace of adulteration include the following:— 
(i) Under the Control Orders issued by the Government to prevent fuel 
adulteration, under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, State Governments 
are empowered to take action against those indulging in adulteration. 
Government have taken up this matter with all the State Governments/Union 
Territory Administrations to step up inspections/surprise checks to ensure that 
adulteration related activities are minimized and to exercise vigil/conduct 
inspections at various private firms, factories, processing units, etc., under their 
jurisdictions so as to identify the perpetrators of adulteration and taken 
stringent action against them within the available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail Outlets and also take 
action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) and Dealership Agreements 
against those indulging in adulteration and malpractices. MDG provide for 
penalty of termination of dealership in cases of adulteration being established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government, Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have created a 
separate wing to report to a Director other than Director (Marketing), which 
will oversee and monitor all activities 
132 

[26 April, 2005) RAJYA SABHA 
and operations to curb adulteration and specify norms and guidelines in 
this regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the import of 
SKO by private parties has been canalized through OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck locking systems to 
prevent en route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) IT solutions like monitoring movement of tank trucks through Global 
Positioning System (GPS) and monitoring level of fuel tanks in Retail Outlets 
through retail automation are being introduced. 
(vB) Branding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail Outlets 
have been initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) A pilot project has been approved for strengthening the distribution network of PDS 
kerosene with a view to working towards ensuring that this product is made 
available to the targeted consumers and is not diverted for adulteration. 
Measures to check adulteration are kept under continuous review of the 
Government.

Governments are empowered to take action against those indulging in 
adulteration. Government have taken up this matter with all the State 
Governments/Union Territory Administrations to step up inspections/surprise 
checks to ensure that adulteration related activities are minimized and to 
exercise vigil/conduct inspections at various private firms, factories, 
processing units, etc., under their jurisdictions so as to identify the perpetrators 
of adulteration and taken stringent action against them within the available 
legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail Outlets and also take 
action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) and Dealership 
Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and malpractices. MDG 
provide for penalty of termination of dealership in cases of adulteration 
being established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government, Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have 
created a separate wing to report to a Director other than 
Director(Marketing), which will oversee and monitor all activities and 
operations to curb adulteration and specify norms and guidelines in this 
regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the import of 
SKO by private parties has been canalized through OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck locking systems to 
prevent en route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) IT solutions like monitoring movement of tank trucks through Global 
Positioning System (GPS) and monitoring level of fuel tanks

in Retail Outlets through retail automation are being introduced. 
(vii) -Branding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail Outlets have 
been initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) A pilot project has been approved for strengthening the distribution network of PDS 
kerosene with a view to working towards ensuring        that this product is made available 
to the targeted consumers and is not diverted for adulteration. 
Measures to check adulteration are kept under continuous review of the 
Government.

(b) if so, whether Government have got any survey made in this regard;

(d) the detailed plans made by Government to improve ground water level and 
funds allotted to States in this regard; and 
(e) the reasons for the pendency of schemes/programmes sent to Government by 
Madhya Pradesh in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) A long-term 
analysis of ground water levels by Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), under the 
Ministry of Water Resources, during the years 1995- 
†Ortginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
2004, indicates decline in ground water levels in some parts of districts of various 
States of the country. The names of these States/districts having pockets of 
declining water level in the last 10 years (1995-2004) are given in the enclosed 
Statement. (See below) 
(d) and (e) "Water" being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments concerned to execute schemes to improve ground water level. 
Presently, there is no approved scheme in the Ministry of Water Resources 
under which funds can be allotted to States for checking the decline in ground 
water level. Hence, no scheme/programme sent by the State Governments, 
including the Government of Madhya Pradesh could be approved. 
However, the following steps have been taken by the Union Government to 
check the decline in ground water levels:- 
(i) CGWB has proposed a scheme at an estimated cost of Rs. 175 
crores for Artificial Recharge to Ground Water and Rain Water 
Harvesting during the remaining part of the X Five Year Plan. 
(ii) Circulation of Manual/Guidelin es on Artificial Recharge of 
Ground Water to the States/Union Territories to enable them to 
formulate area specific artificial recharge schemes to check the 
declining trend of ground water levels. 
(iii) Central Ministries/Departments of Railways, Defence, Posts, 
Telecommunications, Central Public Works Department and 
National Highways Authority of India have been requested to 
provide roof top rain water harvesting structures in the 
buildings under their control. 
(iv) States/UTs have been requested to provide water harvesting 
structures in buildings under their administrative control. 
(v) All the States/Union Territori es have been requested for 
advising the local bodies in their respective States/Union 
Territories to allow rebate in property tax to persons, who 
adopt roof top rainwater harvesting in their premises. 
(vi) CGWB has provided technical guidance on rain water 
harvesting to around 1800 agencies, including State 
Government agencies, educational institutions, private 
entrepreneurs and individuals.

(www.cgwb.net) to make aware and educate the public about various 
techniques of harvesting rainwater and store it for future use. 
(viii) Organisation of mass awareness programmes and training courses on 
rainwater harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(ix) Rain Water Harvesting compaign has been launched keeping in view the 
various target groups like youth and children, women, farmers and 
villages, policy and opinion makers. Publicity through print media, 
telecasting of spots on the television, broadcasting messages on 
radio, holding of seminars, workshops, conferences etc. have

(x) The Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty Alleviation, Government

buildings on plots of 100 square meters and above in Delhi mandatory.

Haryana, Rajasthan and Kerala have made rooftop rain water harvesting 
mandatory in specified cases.

(a) whether Government are aware that the State of Assam faces a serious 
flood situation year after year due to Brahmaputra and Barak river; 
(b) if so, what specific measures Government have taken during the last 
few years to contain floods which causes harm to agriculture and loss of lives 
and property in the State; and 
(c) whether Government have any plan is hand in this regard and if so, the 
details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (c) Yes 
Sir, Flood Management being a State subject, the flood control schemes are planned, 
funded and executed by the State Govt, themselves out of their own resources 
and as per their own priorities. The assistance rendered by Central Government are 
technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. 
Government of India had set up Bhahmaputra Board for preparation of Master 
Plan to control floods, bank erosion and improvement of drainage in the 
Brahmaputra and Barak Valleys also giving due regard to the development 
and utilisation of the Water Resources for irrigation, hydropower, navigation 
and other beneficial use. Accordingly, the Brahmaputra Board undertook 
preparation of the Master Plan and 34 such Master Plans prepared by the Board 
have been sent to the State Government for implementation. 
ATask Force on Flood management/Erosion Control was set up by the 
Government of India in August, 2004 which has since submitted its report. The 
Task force has recommened measures for flood management and suggested 
immediate and short term measures. The report of the Task Force was sent to 
the State Government. 
In order to assist the Government of Assam and the other North Eastern States, 
Government of India has approved a scheme amounting to Rs. 150 crore (90% 
grant and 10% loan) with a share of Rs. 81 crore for Assam for taking up critical 
flood management/anti erosion works. Out of this Rs. 9.3 crore has already 
been released to Assam during the year 2004-05 for ongoing schemes.

21.91 crore at Dholla Hathighuli &

Decline in ground water table in MP 
†3550. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether ground water table has decreased immensely in Madhya Pradesh 
during the last three years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, district-wise; and 
(c) the steps Government are taking to provide relief of common men facing 
the shortage of drinking water as a result of decrese in the ground water level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) An analysis of 
ground water level data by Central Water Board (CGWB), under the Ministry 
of Water Resources, during the last three years (May, 2001 -May, 2004) shows 
declining ground water levels between 2 to 4 meters in parts of Ratlam, Mandsaur, 
Neemuch, Ujjain, Guna, Shajapur, Khandwa, Chhindwara, Seoni, Panna, 
Chhatarpur and Sidhi districts of Madhya Pradesh. Decline of more than 4 
meters has been recorded in parts of Guna, Vidisha, Mandsaur, Ratlam and 
Seoni district of Madhya Pradesh. 
(b) Details of water level fluctuation during the period May, 2001 to May, 2004 
in various districts of Madhya Pradesh have been given in the statement, (see 
below). 
(c) "Water" being a State subject, it is primarily the responsility of the 
concerned State Governments to formulate schemes to provide relief to common 
men facing shortage of drinking water as a result of decrease in the ground water 
level. However, CGWB have constructed 332 exploratory wells under accelerated 
exploratory drilling programme, in drought affected districts of Guna, Sehore, 
Shivpuri, Sheopurkalan, Datia, Gwalior, Chhatarpur, Damoh, Dewas, Morena, 
Panna, Sagar, Tikamgarh, Shajapur and Ujjain in Madya Pradesh during 2001 -02 
to 2004-05. All the successful wells have since been handed over, free of cost, to the 
concerned department of the State Government for utilization for drinking water 
supply purposes. 
Besides, CGWB has also implemented five artificial recharge programmes 
at a cost of Rs. 53.85 lakhs under its Central Sector Scheme "Study of Recharge to 
Ground Water" implemented during the IX Plan.

Problem in Irrigating cultivable Land 
3551. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many areas of the country are drought prone areas, 
and having problem in irrigating cultivable land; 
(b) whether Government have taken initi atives so far to cope with the 
problem, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor, 
(c) whether Government have any plan to inter-linking the rivers of the 
country to provide irrigation water to such areas, if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether Government have made any study of shortage or need of water, 
State-wise, if so, the details thereof and if not, reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Irrigation management in the country including drought prone areas is the 
primarily responsibility of the respective State Governments. Central Government 
supplements these efforts through financial and operational support. In this 
regard, Central Water Commission (CWC) monitors the weekly reservoir levels 
of 76 major reservoirs in the country for assessment of hydrological conditions 
and use by Crop Weather Watch Group of Ministry of Agriculture. The short and 
medium term measures being adopted include rain water harvesting, water-shed 
management and water management in irrigated agriculture. The long term 
measurers include creation of surfact storages and inter-basin transfer of water. 
(c) Ministry of Water Resources (MoWR) erstwhile Ministry of Irrigation) and 
Central Water Commission (CWC) formul ated a Natinal Perspective Plan 
(NPP) for water resource development in 1980 envisaging inter-basin transfer 
of water from surplus basins to deficit basin/area which comprises two 
components namely Himalayan river component and Peninsular Rivers 
Development component, the NPP proposals will help enhancing irrigation 
potential by 35 million hectares and power generation by 34000 MW besides 
providing domestic & industrial water supply, navigation and flood 
moderation benefits etc. Based on various studies, National Water Development 
Agency (NWDA) has identified 30 links for preparing feasibility reports 
(FRs). NWDA has completed feasib ility reports for 16 links and the 
preparation of FRs for remaining links is 
189 
 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
under progress. As per the studies of NWDA, about 2.5 Million hectares of drought 
prone area will be benefited with irrigation from the link proposals. 
(d) The National Water Policy envisages water resources development and 
planning for hydrological unit such as drainage basin as a whole or a sub-basin. 
Accordingly, the water resouces are a ssessed river basin wise and not State-
wise.

Kalsa Bhanduri Nala Scheme 
3553. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Kalsa Bhanduri Nala Scheme sent by the State 
Government of Karnataka is pending with the Central Government for 
approval; 
(b) if so, when the above proposal was sent; 
(c) what is the estimated cost of the above proposal and the extent of land to 
be irrigated from the above scheme; and 
(d) what is the present status of the above proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) The 
Government of Karnataka in April, 2002 requested for clearance of proposal from 
inter-State angle for diversion of 7.56 TMC of water from Madei basin to 
Malprabha basin through implementation of Kalsa and Bhandurinalla schemes 
to meet the drinking water needs of Hubli/Dharwad cities. The proposal was 
not in the form of Detailed Project Report containing the estimated cost and 
other details. The Ministry of Water Resources gave an 'in-principle' clearance 
to the proposal to meet the drinking water need of Hubli/Dharwad from water 
availability angle on 30th April, 2002. The Government of Goa in July, 2002 
took strong exception to the grant of this clearance by the Ministry and requested 
for setting up of an inter-State Water Disputes Tribunal under the Inter-State 
water Disputes Act, 1956 for resolution of the disput. In view of this, the 'in-
principle' clearance granted 
192 

[26 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
by the Ministry was placed 'in abeyance' in September, 2002 with a view to 
resolve the matter by an agreement between the two States, failing which by an 
award of the Tribunal. The two States have so far not concluded any agreement on 
the sharing of Madei Water. 
Implementation of Unauthorised irrigation projects in Krishna and 
Godavari River Basins 
3554. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any all-party delegation from Kamataka has submitted any 
memorandum requesting the Central Government to prevent Andhra Pradesh 
from going ahead with the implementation of unauthorized irrigation projects in 
Krishna and Godavari river basins; and 
(b) if so, what is the present status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. An all 
party delegation led by the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Kamataka, submitted a 
memorandum to His Excellency the Pres ident of India and the then Hon'ble 
Deputy Prime Minister of India in June, 2003 high lighting unilateral action on the 
part of the Government of Andhra Pradesh to commit use of the surplus water of 
Krishna by taking up permanent and large-scale water utilization projects. The State 
Government of Kamataka has reported about submission of another memorandum 
to the Hon'ble Prime Minister of India in February, 2005 during his visit to 
Bangalore, which also highlighted the same issues. 
(b) In response to the complaints and request for apportioning of the surplus 
waters of Krishna among the basin States, the Government of India 
constituted the second Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal on 2nd April, 2004 
to adudicate the disputes on sharing of Krishna Waters among the basin States 
in accordance with the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956. The sharing of the 
Godavari waters among the basin States in on the basis of Godavari Water 
Disputes Tribunal Award, which is an 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2005] 
agglomeration of the agreements on the use of Godavari Waters among the basin 
States. 
Conservation of Water 
3555. SHRI R. GOVINDRAJAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the various schemes launched by Central Government to conserve water keeping 
in view the failure of monsoon frequently; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government propose to initiate new water conservation schemes in 
the country to yield desired results? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Water being 
a state subject, water resources projects including schemes for water conservation are 
planned, executed and maintained by the concerned State Governments. The Government 
of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) for early 
completion of ongoing water resources schemes. Government of India is also promoting 
schemes for rainwater harvesting and recharge to groundwater for conservation of water. 
(d) A pilot scheme"National Project for Repair, Renovation and Restoration of 
Water Bodies Directly Linked to Agriculture" has been approved by the Government of 
India. The objectives of the scheme are to restore and augment the storage capacities of 
water bodies including repair of related structures like checkdams, weirs, bunds and water 
conveyance system and to recover and extend their lost irrigation potential. A scheme on 
"Artificial Recharge to Groundwater and Rainwater Harvesting" is also under active 
consideration of the Government.
